meta.title: Geohistory learning journeys
meta.reviewStatus: Agent source review; independent human scholarly review pending.
meta.scope: Editorial learning paths through existing accepted records; not comprehensive regional coverage.
meta.dateConvention: Signed civil years without year zero. Editorial viewing anchors and approximate travel dates are labeled in each stop.
meta.sourceConvention: Source IDs refer to the included source register and match chronicle.json. A pair of citations is not a count of independent witnesses.
meta.sourceDependencies: ORIAS teaching pages and the linked translations draw on Ibn Battuta’s Rihla; they are related interpretations of one underlying narrative, not independent testimony. UNESCO descriptions and institutional heritage summaries may share scholarship. Quiz answers about map behavior are supported by the shipped dataset and implementation, not by historical sources alone. The 1857 museum narrative and object catalogue both draw on National Army Museum collections; institutional provenance is shared. These learning paths paraphrase bounded facts from the existing atlas and add editorial questions, not newly accepted independent historical claims.
meta.geometryNote: Story lines and connections are schematic. No new territory polygons, precise historical routes, or inferred location coordinates are introduced.

stories.title: When the center moved
stories.subtitle: Damascus · Baghdad · Samarra · Cairo
stories.description: Follow four capitals across three centuries. A new seat of government changed where rulers built, commissioned art, and displayed authority.
stories.takeaway: A shared religious world could contain changing—and competing—political centers.

stops.title: A capital in Syria
stops.description: Under the Umayyads, Damascus became the center of a far-reaching caliphate. Begin here, then watch the center of Abbasid government move east. A change of dynasty was also a change in the geography of power.
stops.question: Which direction will the next capital take you?

stops.title: A new city for a new dynasty
stops.description: The Abbasids established Baghdad as their capital in 762. The move from Syria to Iraq gave the new dynasty a different urban center. Find the Tigris, then compare Baghdad with the earlier capital at Damascus.
stops.question: What does a newly founded capital let a ruler communicate?

stops.title: A court farther up the Tigris
stops.description: Samarra became the Abbasid court’s seat from 836 to 892. Its surviving buildings help historians study a period whose architecture is less visible in Baghdad. The map pin is only a reference point for a much larger archaeological landscape.
stops.question: Why might archaeology tell a different story from a colored territory?

stops.title: Another center of power
stops.description: After taking Egypt in 969, the Fatimids founded Cairo north of Fustat. Cairo’s emergence reminds us that the history of Muslim societies cannot be reduced to a single succession of capitals.
stops.question: Does a new capital mean the older city stopped mattering?

stories.title: Three courts, one connected world
stories.subtitle: Ottoman · Safavid · Mughal
stories.description: Trace the cities of three imperial traditions, then pause on the 1600 map to see their worlds together.
stories.takeaway: Contemporary empires had distinct centers; a single date can reveal more than a sequence of rulers.

stops.title: Constantinople becomes an Ottoman capital
stops.description: The Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453 made the city an imperial center. Keep its western position in mind as this story turns toward Iran and northern India.
stops.question: How does this city’s position compare with the next two centers?

stops.title: A Safavid beginning at Tabriz
stops.description: Ismail I’s accession in 1501 marks the start of Safavid rule. Tabriz gives this dynasty a different starting point from the later capital at Isfahan.
stops.question: Can a dynasty’s first capital explain all of its later geography?

stops.title: Babur enters the north Indian story
stops.description: Babur seized the Delhi Sultanate from Ibrahim Lodi in 1526. Delhi is the political-center marker here, not a pin claiming the precise location of the battle.
stops.question: What is the difference between an event’s battlefield and the political center it affected?

stops.title: A capital reshaped
stops.description: Around 1597–1598, Shah Abbas selected Isfahan as the Safavid capital. Its new civic and ceremonial spaces made imperial authority visible in the city. Move to the 1600 map afterward to compare neighboring powers at one dated moment.
stops.question: What can a city’s buildings tell us that a border cannot?

stops.title: Power, memory, and craftsmanship
stops.description: At Agra, Shah Jahan commissioned the Taj Mahal for Mumtaz Mahal. The principal mausoleum was complete by 1648; the wider complex took longer. This is a building milestone, not a new territorial map.
stops.question: Why should a monument’s completion date stay separate from the map’s reference date?

stories.title: A world seen by a traveler
stories.subtitle: Pilgrimage · service · sea crossings
stories.description: Read four moments from Ibn Battuta’s account. Notice how a pilgrimage becomes a career, then an uncertain voyage.
stories.takeaway: A traveler’s account is a viewpoint. Its route, chronology, and judgments require interpretation.

stops.title: The journey’s first purpose
stops.description: Ibn Battuta describes setting out from Morocco to make the pilgrimage. In 1326 he reached Mecca after traveling through Egypt and the Levant. His route connects sacred places across political boundaries.
stops.question: What makes a pilgrimage route different from an empire’s border?

stops.title: A traveler becomes a judge
stops.description: In Delhi, his account describes service as a judge under Muhammad bin Tughluq. The year shown follows a teaching chronology; his exact arrival date remains unresolved in this atlas.
stops.question: How might employment at a court shape what a traveler writes about it?

stops.title: Plans meet the sea
stops.description: At Calicut, now Kozhikode, Ibn Battuta’s account describes a storm disrupting his intended voyage to China. A port connects people and ambitions, but a line on a map cannot show every delay or reversal.
stops.question: What disappears when a complicated journey becomes one smooth line?
stops.datePrecision: early 1340s; 1342 is an approximate navigation anchor

stops.title: The limits of a visitor’s authority
stops.description: In the Maldives, he describes judicial work and resistance to some of his demands. Read those judgments as the perspective of a visiting jurist, rather than a complete portrait of island society.
stops.question: Whose perspective is missing from this account?
stops.datePrecision: early 1340s; 1343 is an approximate navigation anchor

stories.title: Landscapes of learning
stories.subtitle: Lumbini · Nalanda · Paharpur
stories.description: Look beyond capitals to monuments and monastic institutions in South Asia. These places give the region a history longer and more varied than any one empire.
stories.takeaway: Historical significance can survive changes in rulers, institutions, and the way a place is remembered.

stops.title: A ruler leaves an inscription
stops.description: Ashoka’s visit to Lumbini and its commemorative pillar are conventionally dated to 249 BCE. The inscription is a different kind of historical evidence from a later traveler’s narrative.
stops.question: What can an inscription establish—and what can it leave unanswered?

stops.title: An institution, not a single event
stops.description: Nalanda’s remains include spaces for worship, residence, and teaching. Sources describe it as a center of learning from the fifth century into the medieval period. The year 600 is a viewing anchor within that history, not its foundation date.
stops.question: Why is a long-lived institution difficult to represent with one year?
stops.datePrecision: editorial viewing anchor; not a dated event

stops.title: Patronage and a monastery
stops.description: Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur was a major Buddhist institution associated with the Pala rulers. Foundation traditions differ; this atlas does not turn them into a single exact date. The year 900 is a viewing anchor.
stops.question: How could changing patrons affect a center of learning?
stops.datePrecision: editorial viewing anchor; not a foundation date

stories.title: One city, changing worlds
stories.subtitle: Four moments in Delhi
stories.description: Return to the same place at four dates. Keep the location steady while rulers, institutions, and political meanings change.
stories.takeaway: A city is more than the name of the polity that surrounds its marker.

stops.title: The sultan’s court
stops.description: Ibn Battuta’s account places him in the service of Muhammad bin Tughluq during the 1330s. It gives a visitor’s view of the city’s courtly world. The selected year is approximate.
stops.question: What kind of city do you see when the source is a court visitor?

stops.title: A change of dynasty
stops.description: Babur’s seizure of the Delhi Sultanate in 1526 began Mughal rule. The place remains recognizable on the map while the political story changes.
stops.question: What remains continuous when a ruling dynasty changes?

stops.title: A city in rebellion
stops.description: British forces stormed Delhi in September 1857 during the uprising. This marker selects one city and episode within a much wider conflict; it cannot stand for everyone’s experience of the rebellion.
stops.question: Whose experiences would you seek beyond a military account?

stops.title: Independence and Partition
stops.description: The Indian Independence Act provided for the independent dominions of India and Pakistan. Delhi is a regional navigation anchor, not the whole geography of Partition. Territory borders stay hidden at this date. An optional 1914 reference map is available, but it does not reconstruct 1947 borders.
stops.question: Can the map shown here answer a question about the 1947 boundary?

connections.title: Changing centers of government

connections.title: Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal cities
connections.description: An invitation to compare imperial cities across the region. The cities belong to distinct political histories.
connections.geometryNote: Editorial comparison links, not evidence of a direct road, embassy, or trade route between each pair.

quiz.question: Which city became the new Abbasid capital in 762?
quiz.explanation: Baghdad was founded as the new Abbasid capital in 762. Compare its position in Iraq with the earlier Umayyad center at Damascus.

quiz.question: Which city hosted the Abbasid court between 836 and 892?
quiz.explanation: Samarra’s capital period is documented as 836–892. Its archaeological remains reveal more than a territory color can.

quiz.question: Which dynasty founded Cairo after taking Egypt in 969?
quiz.explanation: The Fatimids founded Cairo in 969. This is one reason to follow several political centers instead of a single line of succession.

quiz.question: Which city became Shah Abbas’s capital around 1597–1598?
quiz.explanation: Isfahan became the Safavid capital around 1597–1598. The atlas uses 1598 as its navigation anchor while retaining the date range.

quiz.question: What does the year 1648 identify in the Taj Mahal record?
options: Completion of every building in the complex
quiz.explanation: The principal mausoleum was complete by 1648; the wider complex developed over a longer period.

quiz.question: What purpose did Ibn Battuta give for leaving Morocco at the start of his travels?
quiz.explanation: His account describes setting out to visit Mecca and Medina. Later court service and sea journeys were parts of a much longer life of travel.

quiz.question: Which place in this atlas was a monastic and teaching institution?
quiz.explanation: Nalanda combined religious and educational life. The date 600 in its story is a viewing anchor, not a claimed foundation year.

quiz.question: At an event dated 1947, you choose “Show 1914 CE reference”. What do those borders represent?
options: The latest available earlier map, dated 1914
The exact borders on the event’s day
quiz.explanation: Narrative dates and territorial evidence are separate. The atlas has a 1947 event but no accepted 1947 territory snapshot.

quiz.question: What do dashed connections between selected journey stops establish?
options: The sequence shown by this atlas
quiz.explanation: The lines are schematic. They omit intermediate stops and do not reconstruct roads, sea lanes, or distances.

quiz.question: How should we read Ibn Battuta’s judgments about Maldivian customs?
options: As the view of every island resident
As the perspective of a visiting jurist
quiz.explanation: The account preserves his viewpoint and describes resistance to some of his demands. Other voices are needed for a fuller history.

periods.title: Ancient worlds
periods.summary: Begin with the region’s long history before Islam: Achaemenid rule at Babylon and Ashoka’s commemorative presence at Lumbini are two selected anchors.
periods.prompt: Compare the different kinds of evidence left by conquest and commemoration.

periods.title: Cities, monasteries, connections
periods.summary: The map’s political outlines tell only one part of the story. Nalanda’s educational life and Bamiyan’s Buddhist heritage point toward other ways to understand the region.
periods.prompt: Open a place record and look for what survives beyond a dynasty.

periods.title: New centers of power
periods.summary: Damascus, Baghdad, Samarra, and Cairo anchor changing governments. In South Asia, monastic institutions such as Somapura offer a different view of patronage and learning.
periods.prompt: Follow the capitals story, then compare it with Paharpur.

periods.title: Across courts and seas
periods.summary: The capture of Baghdad in 1258 and Ibn Battuta’s later travels reveal political rupture alongside continuing urban and long-distance connections.
periods.prompt: Compare the Baghdad event with the traveler’s later description.

periods.title: Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal
periods.summary: Several imperial traditions coexist across the map. Cities, workshops, and monuments make their histories tangible without reducing them to territorial size.
periods.prompt: Start with the 1600 snapshot and compare three courts.

periods.title: Empire and resistance
periods.summary: The atlas’s late-period narrative is selective. Delhi’s 1857 episode offers one entry into rebellion and colonial power; it does not stand for the whole region.
periods.prompt: Ask whose perspective each source represents.

periods.title: Toward independence
periods.summary: The timeline reaches Independence and Partition in 1947. No territory reconstruction is available for that date; the optional 1914 reference does not represent the later boundary settlement.
periods.prompt: Keep the narrative year and territory reference year separate.
